accepted.question_text: For a convex body in Euclidean n-space, must there exist at least n chords whose endpoints are boundary points and such that the body lies on one side of the supporting hyperplane through each endpoint perpendicular to the chord, so that each chord is normal at both endpoints?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Must a convex body in En admit at least n doubly normal chords?
An affirmative solution of the problem is contained in the paper by Kuiper [Kui64] in 1964.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a convex body in Euclidean n-space whose boundary contains a line segment parallel to every direction in the space?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Is there a convex body C in En such that every direction in En is realized by some line segment in the boundary of C?
However, in 1970 the non-existence of such C was established in full generality by Ewald, Larman and Rogers [ELR70].

accepted.question_text: If f and g are commuting continuous self-maps of a closed real interval, must there exist a point in the interval fixed by both maps?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose I is a closed interval of real numbers, and f and g are commuting continuous maps of I into itself. Must they have a common fixed point?

Both published detailed proofs (in 1969 in the same journal [Boy69], [Hun69]) of the negative answer, by constructing examples of pairs of commuting functions that map I into itself but have no common fixed point.

accepted.question_text: If X is a subset of Hilbert space such that every point of the ambient Hilbert space has a unique farthest point in X, must X be a singleton?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose X is a subset of Hilbert space H such that each point of H admits a unique farthest point in X. Must X consist of a single point?
However, the problem as posed by Klee is still – after half a century – open.

accepted.question_text: If Y is a subset of Hilbert space such that every point of the ambient Hilbert space has a unique nearest point in Y, must Y be convex?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose Y is a subset of Hilbert space H such that each point of H admits a unique nearest point in Y . Must Y be convex?
Hiriart-Urruty [HU07] states that (circa 1961) Klee conjectured that the answer is negative for Hilbert space.

accepted.question_text: For integers k and n with k - 1 >= n >= 3, what is the maximum size F(k,n) of a family of convex polyhedra in Euclidean n-space such that every pair intersects in exactly an (n-1)-dimensional set and each polyhedron has at most k vertices?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of integers k and n with k − 1 ≥ n ≥ 3, determine the maximum possible number F(k, n) of neighboring convex polyhedra in En, each having at most k vertices.
The related question about the maximum number f(d, k) of convex d-polytopes in a neighborly family in Ed, each of which has at most k facets, was considered by Zaks [Zak79] in 1979.

accepted.question_text: For a given convex polyhedron P, what is the largest possible number of affine images of P that can form a neighboring family, meaning that every two images intersect in exactly an (n-1)-dimensional set?

evidence.quote: Another unsolved problem is to determine for various convex polyhedra P the maximum possible number of neighboring affine images of P.

accepted.question_text: Let F be the family of closed subsets of Euclidean n-space and K the family of closed convex subsets, with Fi and Ki built by alternating countable increasing unions and countable decreasing intersections. Must every convex member of F2 belong to K4, and more generally how far can convex members of Fi be generated without leaving convexity?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For a family S of subsets of En, let S1 be the family of all sets expressible as the union of an increasing sequence of members of S, S2 the family of all sets expressible as the intersection of a decreasing sequence of members of S1, . . ., S2n+1 the family of all unions of increasing sequences from S2n, S2n+2 the family of all intersections of decreasing sequences from S2n+1, . . . . Let F denote the family of all closed subsets of En, and K the family of all closed convex subsets of En.
Must each convex member of F2 be a member of K4? More generally, determine for each m and i the smallest integer t such that every m-dimensional convex member of Fi is a member of Kt.

accepted.question_text: If BF is the family of Borel subsets of Euclidean n-space and BK is the family generated from closed convex sets by countable increasing unions and decreasing intersections, is every convex Borel set in BF already a member of BK?

evidence.quote: Hence the additional problem: Is every convex member of BF a member of BK?

However, Preiss [Pre73] showed in 1973 that every convex Borel set in any finite-dimensional Banach space may be generated by iteration of countable increasing unions and countable decreasing intersections starting from compact convex sets.

accepted.question_text: For a convex body C in Euclidean n-space, must the nonexposed extreme points form a first-category subset of the extreme points, equivalently, must the boundary contain closed sets J1, J2, ... witnessing that exposed points accumulate at every nonexposed extreme point from outside each Ji containing it?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: If C is a convex body in En, must the boundary of C contain a sequence J1, J2, . . ., of closed sets satisfying the following condition:
For higher dimensions, the problem is open, an affirmative solution being known only when C is smooth [2] and in certain other special cases.

accepted.question_text: For positive integers n and r, what is the smallest number f(n,r) such that every set of f(n,r) points in Euclidean n-space can be partitioned into r pairwise disjoint subsets whose convex hulls share a common point?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of positive integers n and r, determine the smallest integer k(= f(n, r)) such that every set of k points in En can be divided into r pairwise disjoint sets whose convex hulls have a common point.
Birch’s conjecture f(n, r) = (n+1)r−n was affirmatively decided by Tverberg [Tve66].

accepted.question_text: For integers n and r with 0 < r < n, what is the smallest number g(n,r) such that every set of that many points in Euclidean n-space contains an r-dimensional affine flat through r+1 of the points that also intersects the convex hull of the remaining points?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of integers n and r with 0 < r < n, determine the smallest integer k(= g(n, r)) such that for each set of k points in En there is an r-dimensional flat which contains r + 1 of the points and intersects the convex hull of the remaining points.
If n ≤ 2r + 1, I assert that g(n, r) = n + 2.

accepted.question_text: For integers n >= 2 and r >= 3, what is the smallest number h(n,r) such that every set of h(n,r) points in Euclidean n-space contains an r-point subset in which each chosen point lies on the boundary of the convex hull of that subset?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of integers n ≥ 2 and r ≥ 3, determine the smallest integer k(= h(n, r)) such that in each set of k-pointed subsets of En there is an r-pointed set X having each of its points in the boundary of its convex hull.

accepted.question_text: For integers n >= 2 and r >= 3, what is the smallest number h'(n,r) such that every set of h'(n,r) points in general position in Euclidean n-space contains an r-point subset all of whose points are extreme points of its convex hull?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of integers n ≥ 2 and r ≥ 3, determine the smallest integer k(= h′(n, r)) such that in each set of k points in general position in En there is an r-pointed set X having each of its points as an extreme point of its convex hull.

accepted.question_text: Can an n-dimensional convex body admit an expansive homeomorphism, meaning a self-homeomorphism for which some fixed positive distance eventually separates every pair of distinct points under iteration?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Can an n-dimensional convex body admit an expansive homeomorphism?
if the former, then the problem for convex bodies appears to be open in dimensions n ≥ 2.

accepted.question_text: For n >= 2, does there exist an n-dimensional convex body with two distinct equichordal points, that is, two interior points through each of which every chord has the same total length?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: ⋆ Does there exist (for n ≥ 2) an n-dimensional convex body which has two equichordal points?
The accepted wisdom is that the 1997 paper [Ryc97] of Rychlik finally disposed of the problem, by showing that no 2e-curve (of a type that includes convex curves) can have two equichordal points.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a plane convex body with two equireciprocal points, meaning two interior points p for which the quantity |x-p|^{-1} + |y-p|^{-1} is constant over all chords [x,y] through p?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Does there exist (for n = 2) an n-dimensional convex body which has two equireciprocal points?

With the approaching century-mark since the problem was first proposed, it would be even more enjoyable and desirable to have an independent confirmation – or rebuttal – of the results and claims of Helfenstein and Wirsing, and a clarification of the status of the problem and its solution.

accepted.question_text: Suppose K is a convex cone in Euclidean n-space, H is a hyperplane whose section H ∩ K is an (n-1)-dimensional convex body of constant width, and another hyperplane H' has the property that the orthogonal projection onto H of H' ∩ K also has constant width. Must H and H' be parallel?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose K is a convex cone in En, H a hyperplane whose intersection with K is an (n−1)-dimensional convex body of constant width, and H′ is a hyperplane such that the orthogonal projection onto H of the set H′ ∩ K is also of constant width. Must H be parallel to H′ ?

accepted.question_text: For bounded subsets of Euclidean n-space, is it always possible to cover the set by n+1 subsets of smaller diameter, equivalently for convex bodies of constant width, can each such body be covered by n+1 closed sets none of which contains an antipodal pair?

evidence.quote: Of the problems suggested above, determination of fWn is the most interesting, due to its connection with the following problem of Borsuk [2]: Can every bounded subset of En be covered by n + 1 subsets of smaller diameter?
But it is remarkable that the problem is still unsolved in the case 4 ≤ n ≤ 322.

accepted.question_text: For a class K of convex bodies, what is the largest integer gK such that some body in K contains gK points that are pairwise antipodal, meaning every two lie in parallel supporting hyperplanes of the body?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For various classes K of convex bodies, determine the largest integer k(= gK) such that some member of K contains k points which are pairwise antipodal.
Concerning gK, besides the facts mentioned by Klee, it was established in [DG62] that gCn = 2n for all n.

accepted.question_text: If a compact set X in Euclidean n-space has the property that every point of X lies in a unique minimal convex visibility set, must X contain a point from which every point of X is visible, i.e. must X be star-shaped from some point?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose X is a compact subset of En such that each point of X lies in a unique minimal convex set of visibility. Must X include a point of visibility?

accepted.question_text: What is the smallest integer Dn such that Euclidean n-space can be covered by Dn sets, none of which contains two points at unit distance?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each integer n > 1, determine the smallest integer k(= Dn) such that the n-dimensional Euclidean space En can be covered by k sets, none of which includes two points at unit distance.
With all of this, the original problem is still open even for n = 2, where it is only known that 4 ≤ k ≤ 7.

accepted.question_text: For n >= 2, can Euclidean n-space be covered by countably many sets S1, S2, ... such that no single Si contains two distinct unordered point-pairs at the same nonzero distance?

evidence.quote: It is not known whether En admits such a covering for n ≥ 2.

accepted.question_text: If K' and K are centrally symmetric convex bodies in Euclidean n-space with the same center, and every central hyperplane section of K' has (n-1)-dimensional volume at most that of the corresponding section of K, must the n-dimensional volume of K' be at most that of K?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose K′ and K are n-dimensional convex bodies with a common center of symmetry p. Suppose further that for each hyperplane H through p, the (n − 1)-dimensional area of the section K′ ∩ H is less than or equal to that of the section K ∩ H. Must the n-dimensional volume of K′ be less than or equal to that of K?
However, it turned out (see [Zha99]) that Zhang’s proof is valid only for n ≥ 5, and that for n = 4 the problem has an affirmative solution.
The first result was by Larman and Rogers [LR75] in 1975; they provided a negative answer for all dimensions n ≥ 12.

accepted.question_text: If centrally symmetric convex bodies K' and K in Euclidean n-space have every (n-1)-dimensional orthogonal projection of K' no larger than the corresponding projection of K, must the volume of K' be no larger than the volume of K?

evidence.quote: If K′ and K are centrally symmetric convex bodies in En such that the projection of K′ on any (n−1)-dimensional hyperplane has (n − 1)-content that is smaller than or equal to that of the projection of K, is the n-dimensional volume of K′ necessarily smaller than or equal to the volume of K?
As shown by Petty [Pet67] and Schneider [Sch67], the answer is affirmative for n = 2 and negative for n ≥ 3.

accepted.question_text: If 2 <= k < n and C is a centered convex body in Euclidean n-space such that all of its central k-dimensional sections are affinely equivalent to one another, must C be an ellipsoid?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose 2 ≤ k < n, and C is an n-dimensional centered convex body of which all central k-sections are affinely equivalent. Must C be an ellipsoid?
The quest for characterizations of ellipsoids continues unabated, with too many and too diverse approaches to give details here.

accepted.question_text: If C is a three-dimensional centered convex body all of whose central plane sections are projectively equivalent, must C be an ellipsoid?

evidence.quote: Specifically, if C is a 3-dimensional centered convex body of which all central plane sections are projectively equivalent, must C be an ellipsoid? Süss’s problem appears still to be open.
Corollary 3.3.5 in Thompson’s book [Tho96] presents a solution of Süss’s problem for all n ≥ 3, utilizing the Löwner ellipsoid.

accepted.question_text: If C is a centered convex body and for every central hyperplane section S the maximum volume VS of a cone with base S and apex on the boundary of C is the same, must C be an ellipsoid?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Let C be an n-dimensional centered convex body, and for each central (n − 1)-section S of C let VS be the maximum volume attained by the cones which are based on S and have vertex in the boundary of C. If VS has the same value for all S, must C be an ellipsoid?
(The answer is negative for n = 2 [3], and the problem is open for n ≥ 3)

accepted.question_text: If C is a centered convex body and for every boundary point p together with every central hyperplane section S maximizing the cone volume from p, the quotient Rp,S between the projected area A1 and the section area A2 is constant, must C be an ellipsoid?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose C is an n-dimensional centered convex body, and consider all pairs (S, p) such that p is a boundary point of C and S, among the central (n − 1)-sections of C, is one which maximizes the volume of the cone from p over S.
Then if Rp,S has the same value for all p and S as described, must C be an ellipsoid?

accepted.question_text: Must every Jordan curve in the plane contain four points that are the vertices of a square?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Must a Jordan curve contain the vertices of a square?
As far as I can tell, the original problem is still open, although it has been answered in the affirmative for many special types of curves.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a universal side length d with 0 < d < 1 such that for every continuous real-valued function on the unit square, the graph of the function contains the four vertices of a square of side length d?

evidence.quote: Does there exist a positive number d < 1 such that i) for each continuous function f on S, the graph of f contains the vertices of a square of side d?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a universal side length d with 0 < d < 1 such that for every continuous function on the unit square that vanishes on the boundary, the graph contains the vertices of a square of side length d parallel to the base square?

evidence.quote: ii) for each continuous function f on S which vanishes everywhere on B, the graph of f contains the vertices of a square of side d which is parallel to the plane of S?

accepted.question_text: For a point p inside an n-simplex S, if Di denotes the sum of distances from p to the i-dimensional faces of S, what universal inequalities must hold among the quantities Di for all choices of p and S?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose p is a point of an n-dimensional simplex S, and for 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1, let Di denote the sum of the distances from p to the various i dimensional faces of S. What relations among the numbers Di must persist for all p and S as described?

accepted.question_text: For a tetrahedron and an interior point p, is the sum D0 of distances from p to the vertices always greater than sqrt(8) times D2, the sum of distances from p to the four faces?

evidence.quote: In particular, if n = 3 (so that S is a tetrahedron) is it true that i) D0 > √8D2 (D. K. Kazarinoff) ?

accepted.question_text: For a tetrahedron and an interior point p, is the sum D0 of distances from p to the vertices always greater than D1, the sum of distances from p to the edges?

evidence.quote: ii) D0 > D1 (A. Shields) ?

accepted.question_text: For a tetrahedron and an interior point p, is the sum D1 of distances from p to the edges always greater than 2 times D2, the sum of distances from p to the faces?

evidence.quote: iii) D1 > 2D2 (N. D. Kazarinoff and A. Shields) ?

accepted.question_text: For a plane convex body C, if Dθ(C) is the longest chord joining two supporting rays that meet at angle θ and Wθ(C) is the shortest such chord, what is the greatest lower bound of Dπ/2(C) divided by D0(C) over all plane convex bodies?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Study the class of plane convex bodies C in terms of the θ-diameter Dθ(C) and the θ-width Wθ(C). In particular, determine the greatest lower bound of the quotient Dπ/2/D0.

accepted.question_text: Suppose F is a family of subsets of Euclidean n-space closed under arbitrary intersections, translations, and point reflections, and containing some nonempty bounded open set. Must F also contain a nondegenerate convex set?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Suppose F is a family of subsets of En which includes each intersection of a subfamily of its members, each translate of one of its members, and each point-reflection of one of its members. Then if F includes some nonempty bounded open set, must F include some nondegenerate convex sets?
The higher-dimensional case seems still to be open; I conjecture that the answer is negative for all dimensions ≥ 3.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a triangle whose side lengths, three median lengths, and area are all integers?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: Does there exist a triangle which has integral sides, medians, and area?
The problem appears to be still unsolved, but an affirmative solution was found to the modified question in which only two of the medians are required to be integral.

accepted.question_text: For integers n and r with 2 <= n <= r, what is the smallest possible dimension Af(n,r), respectively Sf(n,r), of a convex polyhedron P such that every n-dimensional convex polyhedron with r+1 maximal faces is affinely equivalent, respectively similar, to a proper section of P?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each pair of integers n and r with 2 ≤ n ≤ r, determine the smallest possible dimension Af(n, r) (resp. Sf(n, r)) of a convex polyhedron P such that every n-dimensional convex polyhedron having r + 1 maximal faces is affinely equivalent (resp. similar) to some proper section of P.

accepted.question_text: If the facet-count condition in the universal section problem is replaced by a vertex-count condition, what are the corresponding minimum dimensions Av, Sv, ξa,v, and ξs,v for realizing every n-dimensional convex polyhedron with r+1 vertices as a proper section up to affine equivalence or similarity?

evidence.quote: Rather than considering the functions Af, Sf, ξa,f, and ξs,f defined above, it is perhaps more natural to consider functions Av, Sv, ξa,v, ξs,v, whose definitions are obtained from those above by replacing “r +1 maximal faces” with “r +1 vertices”.

accepted.question_text: For a closed convex set C in Euclidean n-space, let αC be the set of dimensions j in {1,...,n-1} for which C admits a j-dimensional asymptote, that is, a j-flat disjoint from C but containing points arbitrarily close to C. Which subsets of {1,...,n-1} can occur as αC?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM: For each n-dimensional closed convex subset C of En, let αC denote the set of all integers j between 1 and n − 1 such that C admits a j-asymptote. Determine what subsets of {1, . . ., n − 1} can be realized as the set αC for some C in En.
In a later paper [Kle67], Klee gave a complete answer to the problem: Every subset of {1, 2, . . ., n−1} is the set αC for some convex body C in Euclidean n-space.
